To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the administration of T3 to rats in vivo increases protein phosphorylation in liver nuclei and cytosol, that this effect is not due to an increase in ATP synthesis, that the effect on nuclear proteins is due primarily to a stimulation of the phosphorylation of nonhistone proteins, and that the effect is mediated by a T3 receptor that is not identical to the T3 receptor that binds to the nucleus and stimulates RNA synthesis.
The administration of T3 to hypothyroid rats results in a progressive increase in the rate of phosphorylation of nuclear proteins.

T3 administration in vivo increases 32Pi incorporation in all nuclear protein fractions, with the greatest increase in globulins, and the greatest response in histones, which are phosphorylated by the end of the experiment.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of thyroid hormone on the metabolism of nuclear proteins.
the effects of thyroid hormones on protein phosphorylation in liver nuclei.
the effect of thyroid hormone on the metabolism of liver nuclear proteins in vivo.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

triiodothyronin stimulates the incorporation of 32P into liver proteins in vivo in hypothyroid rats and that the increase in 32P incorporation is due to an increased rate of 32P transfer to protein from the cytosolic phosphate pool and not from the cytosol in vivo.
T3 administration induces an increased phosphorylation of nuclear proteins in rat liver.
the effect of T3 on nuclear protein phosphorylation is complex, and that the effect is not confined to a single protein fraction.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
T3 administration to hypothyroid rats induced a rapid and progressive increase in the phosphorylation of nuclear nonhistone proteins, histone H1, histone H2A, and histone H4.

the incorporation of [32Pi] into liver nuclear proteins in vivo is reduced by 15-35% in hypophysectomized rats compared to controls, and is increased by triiodothyronin (T3) administration in hypothyroid rats.
T3 administration in vivo induced a progressive increase, in the specific activity of nuclear proteins, which was maximal 6–12 h after injection.
The main takeaway from our work is that
T3 has a profound effect on the phosphorylation state of nuclear nonhistone proteins, which is reflected in the incorporation of 32Pi into nuclear proteins in vivo.
the liver is the major site of T3 action in vivo, that the nuclear protein kinase activity is the primary target of T3, and that the nuclear kinase is activated by T3 in vivo.
thyroid hormone has an important regulatory role on the nuclear proteins.
